attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, said in his voice and not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense observation about a trend, plus a qualified 'not clear' clause about IP. Reading 'here' as OpenAI/LLMs fits the context. No horizon or conditions were dropped.

contract.note: The plain reading (movement toward substitutes, without requiring full interchangeability) is ordinary and fair. Using 2022 as the target period is the evaluator's choice but reasonable. Reading the IP clause as uncertainty, not a claim that no IP exists, matches Marcus's words.

evidence.note: May–June 2022 OPT paper reports technical parity with GPT-3. This supports the capability trend but does not show commercial substitution.
November 2022 BLOOM v1 reports competitive benchmark results from an open-access model, which supports more available alternatives.
OpenAI's dated pricing record shows a roughly two-thirds Davinci price cut from Sept 2022, i.e. falling access cost. It covers a single vendor only.

Independent HELM evaluation: open models improved dramatically but still lag closed ones, models are not yet interoperable, and tuning methods are undisclosed. It cuts both ways and settles neither clause.
OPT's noncommercial license limits its use as a practical commercial substitute, which narrows what e1 shows.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows a fast technical trend in 2022: comparable open models, dramatic improvement, and lower OpenAI prices. But the contract asks for substantial movement toward practical substitutes in ordinary uses. HELM says models are not yet interoperable and open models lag, and OPT is noncommercial. No source measures practical switching. Nothing clearly establishes an exclusive OpenAI advantage, so the IP clause is not contradicted, but it is not settled either.
